abstract:
The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM’s own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods.

Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

sections.body: Stylized hair in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Realistic-hair generators output strands, and image-to-3D generators output one fused mesh with no cards. CHARM is the only generator of stylized hair cards, and it decodes each hairstyle as a long sequence of control points. HairDeck gives each card one token holding a latent from a card VAE, its root position, root normal and cross-section type. A set diffusion transformer denoises all tokens together, and a second set generates the spring-bone chains. On CHARM's test set, HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and runs 33 times faster.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing generators do not output the artist-placed hair cards of stylized characters, so HairDeck generates each card as one token.

sections.body: Related work falls into five groups. Strand methods reconstruct or generate realistic hair, and recent ones accept stylized images but still output strands. Card methods convert strands into alpha-textured cards for realistic hair, and CHARM introduced stylized cards with an autoregressive transformer. Stylized character methods fuse hair into a continuous surface or treat it as a separate component. Set and structured generators, including 3DTopia-XL and StrokeFusion, generate the elements of an asset together, and the paper builds on this set formulation. Rigging methods such as UniRig and DRiVE predict spring bones for existing assets, whereas HairDeck generates the chains together with the cards.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work covers strand hair, realistic cards, stylized characters and set generation, but CHARM is the only prior stylized card generator.

sections.body: Each card is a polyline of control points with width and thickness, plus a cross-section type and a root normal. A card VAE encodes its control points into a 32-dimensional latent and decodes the card at uniformly spaced arc-length fractions. A card token holds the root position, root normal, latent, cross-section type and existence flag, which gives a 40-dimensional token, and a hairstyle is a set of 192 slots. The set diffusion transformer has no positional embedding, so no card order is defined, and it is trained with flow matching. A single image conditions the model through DINOv3 features in a face-anchored head frame. A chain diffusion transformer then generates spring-bone chains from the card tokens.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Each card is encoded as one continuous token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all tokens together without positional embedding.

sections.body: On point clouds, under CHARM's protocol, HairDeck reaches a Chamfer distance of 0.0066 against 0.0117 for CHARM, and an orientation error of 16.8° against 40.0°, at 1.01 s against 33.7 s per hairstyle. Card-level autoregressive generation of the same tokens reaches 0.0078, so generating them as a set lowers Chamfer distance further. On single images, the aligned Chamfer distance is 0.0089 against 0.0139 to 0.0186 for the other methods, and the failure rate on test characters is 3.5% against 13.2% to 34.2%. In the ablations, removing the root normal raises orientation error from 16.8° to 26.4°, and a smaller 54.6M-parameter model keeps the Chamfer distance at 0.0072.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On CHARM's test set HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance from 0.0117 to 0.0066 and orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, taking 1.01 s.

sections.body: HairDeck generates the geometry and texture coordinates of the cards but no textures. It learns from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so very short hair and the alpha-textured cards of realistic hair lie outside its training data. Some VRoid characters model bows and hats as hair cards, which HairDeck generates when the input shows them, and filtering such cards from the training data would avoid this. The chain model follows the chain layouts common among VRoid characters and generates fewer chains for unusual ones, such as many chains radiating from the crown. Figure 23 shows failure cases. The conclusion argues that assets built from other artist-defined primitives, such as garments sewn from panels or drawings made of strokes, can be generated in the same way.
sections.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
sections.headline: HairDeck outputs card geometry without textures and learns only from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so short hair and realistic cards fall outside it.

sections.body: The appendix gives training settings for the card VAE, the set diffusion transformer and the chain model, including 80K steps for the card VAE. It describes the synthetic appearance augmentations, the restyled training renders, and the head-frame constants. It defines the chain metrics, the motion protocol, the skinning thresholds, and how cards are exported to VRM. It also details the baselines: the card-level autoregressive model, retrieval, the procedural rig, the mesh generators, the DiffLocks conversion into 60 cards, and the image-to-3D cascades. The last parts report the cascade table, the drawing-style table and the failure cases.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists implementation settings, appearance augmentation, chain metrics, export, baseline details, and additional comparisons and results.
